content.overview: BSA s. 1, Short title, application and commencement, is an evidentiary provision in the Preliminary cluster. Analyse it through the separate questions of relevancy, admissibility, proof, burden and probative weight, and check BSA s. 170 for proceedings governed by the repeal and savings rule.

content.study:
Current-law identity
BSA s. 1 governs short title, application and commencement within Chapter I - Preliminary. The provision must be read with its enacted clauses, explanations, illustrations and connected provisions BSA s. 2.

The forensic distinction
Relevancy asks whether a fact has the statutory connection required by the Adhiniyam. Admissibility asks whether the Court may receive that relevant material under the rules of exclusion, privilege, form and foundation. Proof asks whether the admitted material establishes the fact to the required standard. Probative weight asks how much reliance the Court should place on it. A relevant fact is not automatically admissible, and admissibility is not proof of the ultimate fact.

Mandatory application checklist
1. Identify the fact in issue, the fact sought to be introduced and the party tendering it.
2. State the exact rule in BSA s. 1, including every condition, explanation, proviso and illustration.
3. Classify the material as oral, documentary, electronic, real or circumstantial evidence.
4. Test directness, hearsay, privilege, primary or secondary evidence, authentication and statutory certificate requirements.
5. Identify the party bearing the initial burden under BSA s. 104 and any special-knowledge rule under s. 109.
6. Separate admissibility from the weight ultimately assigned after cross-examination and the complete record.

Electronic records and constitutional limits
Electronic and digital records are documents under BSA. Where a computer output, email, messaging record, CCTV export, call record, server log or device image is tendered through the statutory route, check BSA s. 63 and its certificate requirements. The certificate is not a substitute for relevance, authenticity, chain of custody or proof of the fact asserted. Evidence must also respect Articles 20(3), 21 and 14 of the Constitution, privilege rules and fair-trial disclosure.

Courtroom method
In a written submission, identify the fact in issue, show the statutory relevancy link, answer the admissibility objection, establish the foundation, identify the burden and standard, and explain the probative consequence. Do not cite the historical Evidence Act number as the current rule after 1 July 2024 except as concordance. Do not convert a missing certificate, hearsay statement or weak foundation into an automatic finding on the merits without analysing the applicable statutory consequence.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective and Evidentiary Foundation
sections.body:
BSA s. 1 regulates short title, application and commencement within Preliminary.
The statutory scheme seeks reliable adjudication by limiting proof to legally relevant and properly received material.
Read the provision with the constitutional values of fair trial, privilege, reliability and equality of arms.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Exceptions and Connected Rules
sections.body:
Deconstruct every clause of BSA s. 1; do not replace the enacted rule with a one-line Evidence Act summary.
Read it with BSA s. 2. Connected provisions may control foundation, exclusion, presumptions, witnesses or the mode of proof.
Historical concordance assists comparison only and is not the current citation.

sections.heading: Mandatory Relevancy, Admissibility and Proof Ingredients
sections.body:
First ingredient: identify the fact in issue or the statutory relevancy link.
Second ingredient: satisfy any exclusion, privilege, directness, primary-document or foundation rule.
Third ingredient: prove authenticity and the source or maker where the form of evidence requires it.
Fourth ingredient: apply the correct burden and standard, then distinguish admissibility from probative weight.

sections.heading: BSA Burdens, Presumptions and Electronic Records
sections.body:
BSA s. 104 supplies the ordinary burden framework; the party asserting the legal proposition must establish its foundation.
BSA s. 109 addresses facts especially within knowledge. It does not erase the initial burden or permit conviction on an unproved charge.
For electronic records, examine BSA s. 63 certificate, device or system identity, production method, integrity, custody and the distinction between admissibility and weight.

sections.heading: Trial Roadmap, Forum, Limitation and Repeal Savings
sections.body:
Apply BSA s. 1 at the correct stage of trial or inquiry and identify whether the objection concerns tender, marking, admissibility, proof or final weight.
For proceedings governed by the post-1 July 2024 evidence regime, cite BSA. For proceedings saved by s. 170, identify the applicable Indian Evidence Act route before arguing the consequence.
Check the governing procedural statute and any special limitation rule for the application or appeal; evidence law itself does not create a universal limitation period.

provisions.title: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

examples.title: Example 1 - Foundation and admissibility satisfied
examples.body: A party identifies the fact in issue, establishes the statutory relevancy link under s. 1, proves the source and authenticity of the record, and satisfies the applicable documentary or electronic foundation. The Court may receive the material and then assess its weight.

examples.title: Example 2 - Relevancy does not cure a defect
examples.body: A party offers a relevant screenshot or hearsay statement but cannot satisfy the applicable statutory foundation, certificate, directness or privilege rule. The Court must analyse admissibility separately instead of treating logical relevance as automatic proof.

hypotheticals.question: Whether the material is relevant and admissible under BSA s. 1, and what proof and burden consequences follow.
hypotheticals.analysis: 1. Identify the fact in issue and the statutory relevancy route. 2. Test the form of evidence: direct oral evidence, documentary evidence, electronic record, hearsay or privileged communication. 3. Check the applicable foundation and BSA s. 63 certificate where digital material is tendered. 4. Place the initial burden under s. 104 and use s. 109 only after the foundation for special knowledge is established. 5. Separate admissibility from credibility and final probative weight.

distinctions.title: BSA s. 1: relevancy, admissibility and proof

rows.right: Connected relevancy, foundation, burden or exclusion rule

rows.left: What fact or evidentiary act does this section govern?
rows.right: What additional condition must be satisfied?

rows.left: Apply the section to the tendered material
rows.right: Then decide admissibility, credibility and weight separately

misconceptions.trap: Citing only the old Evidence Act number for s. 1.
misconceptions.correction: Use BSA s. 1 for the current regime and mention the historical number only as concordance or when applying the s. 170 savings rule.

misconceptions.trap: Relevancy automatically means admissibility and proof.
misconceptions.correction: Relevancy, admissibility, proof and probative weight are separate forensic inquiries.

misconceptions.trap: BSA s. 109 reverses the entire burden of proof.
misconceptions.correction: The initial burden remains with the party asserting the legal proposition; special knowledge operates only on the facts within that statutory rule.

cases.name: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
cases.facts: The case concerned the proof and certification of electronic records tendered in election litigation.
cases.issue: Whether the statutory certificate requirement for computer outputs is mandatory and when secondary electronic evidence may be received.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The certificate requirement is a condition precedent for admissibility of the relevant electronic record output, subject to the statutory route and the Court's power to facilitate production where the facts justify it.
cases.holding: The Constitution Bench clarified the certificate rule and overruled the contrary view to the extent necessary.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 1 concerns electronic records or digital proof; it does not decide the relevancy or admissibility of every non-digital item.

cases.name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
cases.facts: The Court examined the mode of proving electronic records in an election dispute.
cases.issue: Whether electronic records could be admitted without compliance with the statutory certificate route.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Electronic evidence must be proved through the special statutory requirements applicable to computer outputs; ordinary secondary-evidence principles cannot bypass that route.
cases.holding: The earlier contrary approach was displaced and the certificate discipline was reaffirmed.
cases.relevance: Use only for digital evidence issues connected with s. 1; distinguish it from ordinary oral, physical-document or privilege questions.

cases.name: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra
cases.facts: The Court assessed a prosecution based substantially on circumstantial evidence.
cases.issue: What standard must circumstantial evidence meet before it can support a criminal conviction.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive in tendency, and form a complete chain excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
cases.holding: The Court restated the safeguards for conviction on circumstantial evidence.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 1 concerns circumstantial proof or inference; do not use it as a substitute for a section-specific relevancy rule.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Provide a structured legal brief on BSA s. 1 - Short title, application and commencement.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE AND EVIDENTIARY QUESTION
Identify the fact in issue, the material tendered and the objection or statutory route.

II. RULE
BSA s. 1 governs short title, application and commencement. Read it with BSA s. 2, then identify the relevancy, admissibility, proof and burden rules.

III. APPLICATION
Test foundation, directness, privilege, documentary or electronic requirements, BSA s. 63 where applicable, and burdens under ss. 104 and 109.

IV. CONCLUSION
State whether the material is relevant, admissible, proved and what weight or procedural consequence follows.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: IRAC brief separating relevancy, admissibility, proof, burden and weight.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Draft written submissions on BSA s. 1 - Short title, application and commencement.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. FACTUAL AND EVIDENTIARY PROVENANCE
Identify the witness, document, digital record, fact in issue and stage of tender.

II. STATUTORY SCHEME
Deconstruct BSA s. 1, its Chapter, connected provisions BSA s. 2 and s. 170 savings.

III. RELEVANCY AND ADMISSIBILITY
Show the statutory connection, answer hearsay or privilege objections, establish the appropriate foundation and address BSA s. 63 for electronic records.

IV. BURDEN, STANDARD AND WEIGHT
Apply BSA ss. 104 and 109 without reversing the initial burden, then distinguish admissibility from credibility and probative weight.

V. PRECEDENTS AND PRAYER
Apply only relevant verified ratios and seek a precise ruling on tender, marking, exclusion, further foundation or final reliance.

learningObjectives: Master the short title, territorial extent, and institutional application of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 under Section 1.
Understand the definition and scope of "judicial proceedings in or before any Court" including Courts-martial.
Analyze the two critical statutory exclusions: non-application to affidavits presented to any Court or officer, and non-application to proceedings before an arbitrator.
Examine the appointed date of commencement (1 July 2024) and the savings transition under Section 170.
enhancement.definition: BSA s. 1 establishes the short title, extent, application, and commencement of the Adhiniyam. It provides that the Act may be called the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; extends to the whole of India; applies to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court, including Courts-martial (other than Courts-martial convened under the Army Act, Naval Discipline Act, or Air Force Act); expressly does not apply to affidavits presented to any Court or officer, nor to proceedings before an arbitrator; and came into force on 1 July 2024.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The uniform codification of the law of judicial evidence, balancing strict rules of proof in adversarial judicial forums against the flexible, expeditious, and equitable procedures governing arbitrations and affidavit evidence.
statutoryFramework: Sub-section (1): Short title — Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
Sub-section (2): Extends to the whole of India.
Sub-section (2) Application Clause: Applies to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court, including Courts-martial.
Sub-section (2) Exclusionary Proviso: Does not apply to affidavits presented to any Court or officer, nor to proceedings before an arbitrator.
Sub-section (3): Commencement on appointed date (1 July 2024) via Central Government notification.
essentialIngredients: Short Title: Enacted as the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Act No. 47 of 2023).
Territorial Jurisdiction: Extends throughout the whole of India, replacing the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
Forum Test: Applies strictly to "judicial proceedings in or before any Court" (where evidence is or may be legally taken on oath).

Dual Statutory Exclusions: (1) Affidavits are excluded from the BSA (governed by procedural codes CPC Order XIX / BNSS s. 329); (2) Arbitral proceedings are excluded (governed by Section 19, Arbitration & Conciliation Act, 1996).
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 1 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 defines the institutional and jurisdictional reach of India’s law of evidence. It replaces Section 1 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 while maintaining the classical demarcations of evidentiary jurisprudence.

The BSA applies to all "judicial proceedings in or before any Court". Under Section 2(1)(i) BNSS, a judicial proceeding includes any proceeding in the course of which evidence is or may be legally taken on oath. Thus, the strict exclusionary rules of the BSA (hearsay rules, confession exclusions, and best evidence requirements) bind trial courts, appellate courts, and Courts-martial (except service-specific disciplinary courts).

Equally vital are the two express statutory exclusions under Section 1(2):
1. **Affidavits:** An affidavit is not "evidence" under Section 2(1)(e) BSA because it is not an oral statement made before the court nor a document subjected to immediate cross-examination. Affidavits are governed by procedural rules: Order XIX of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and Section 329 BNSS. Where a statute expressly permits proof by affidavit (e.g., formal evidence of officials), the court may receive it, but the general rules of the BSA do not govern affidavits per se.
2. **Arbitral Proceedings:** Arbitration is an alternative dispute resolution mechanism designed for speed, flexibility, and party autonomy. Section 19(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 explicitly confirms that the arbitral tribunal is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure or the law of evidence. Arbitrators must follow natural justice and procedural fairness, but cannot be constrained by the technical evidentiary hurdles of the BSA.
examples: Teaching illustration (Exclusion of Strict Evidence in Arbitration): In a commercial arbitration involving a infrastructure contract, the claimant submits an uncertified photocopy of an internal email. The respondent objects, arguing the document violates Section 63 BSA. The Arbitrator overrules the objection: under Section 1(2) BSA read with Section 19 of the Arbitration Act, 1996, the strict technical rules of the BSA do not apply to arbitral proceedings; the tribunal evaluates the document on principles of natural justice and relevance.

Teaching illustration (Affidavit as Substantive Evidence in Criminal Trial): In a murder trial, the prosecution seeks to prove the eyewitness testimony of a witness by tendering a sworn affidavit without producing the witness for oral examination. The defence objects. The Sessions Judge excludes the affidavit: under Section 1(2) BSA, affidavits are excluded from the BSA, and criminal guilt cannot be proved by untested affidavits in place of oral evidence under oath.
distinctions: BSA s. 1 vs IEA 1872 s. 1: BSA s. 1 modernizes references to the new procedural codes (BNSS and BNS) and confirms the universal territorial application to the whole of India post-2019.
BSA s. 1 vs CPC Order XIX / BNSS s. 329: BSA s. 1 excludes affidavits from the definition of evidence, leaving the verification, format, and reception of affidavits entirely to procedural statutes.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a party in a civil suit can prove the terms of a contested oral family settlement solely through an affidavit of a deceased relative without satisfying the exceptions of Section 26 BSA.
Rule: Under Section 1(2) BSA, the Adhiniyam does not apply to affidavits; an affidavit does not become substantive evidence unless permitted by procedural law or subjected to cross-examination.
Application: The relative is deceased and cannot be cross-examined. The affidavit does not fall within the specific dying declaration or statement-in-course-of-business exceptions of Section 26 BSA.
Conclusion: The affidavit cannot be received as substantive proof of the contested oral settlement under the BSA.

shortAnswer: State the short title, extent (whole of India), and commencement date (1 July 2024).
State the core application: all judicial proceedings in or before any Court.
List the two vital statutory exclusions: affidavits and arbitral proceedings.

keyTakeaways: BSA s. 1 extends to the whole of India and took effect on 1 July 2024.
Applies to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court.
Expressly does not apply to affidavits presented to any Court or officer.
Expressly does not apply to proceedings before an arbitrator.
